Jhalak Live: where did the repeat buyers go?

Mumbai, August 2026. A live-commerce company has lost 6.6 points of repeat purchase in four months. Three people have three explanations, each with a different bill attached.

1. Monday morning, Lower Parel

On Monday 3 August 2026, Sneha Vaidya arrived at Jhalak Live's office above a mill compound in Lower Parel with four days to settle an argument that had been running since May. The festive plan — the media budget, the operations staffing and the engineering roadmap for Ganesh Chaturthi through Diwali — had to be locked on Friday 7 August. Three-quarters of Jhalak's annual profit was made in those ten weeks, and the plan she signed on Friday could not be meaningfully changed after the second week of September.

The problem was a single number. Among customers making their first purchase on Jhalak, the share who bought again within thirty days had been 31.1 per cent across December to March. Across April to July it was 24.5 per cent. Six and a half points, on roughly 2.9 lakh first-time buyers a month and an average order value of ₹1,850, was not a detail. If the April-to-July rate held through the festive season, Jhalak would end the year with something in the region of ₹95 crore less gross merchandise value than the plan assumed.

2. The company

Jhalak Live sold ethnic wear — sarees, lehengas, kurta sets, occasion jewellery — through live video. Hosts broadcast forty-minute shows from a studio floor in Surat, holding fabric to the camera, quoting prices, answering questions in Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi and Tamil, while viewers tapped to buy without leaving the stream. Founded in 2021 by two former textile wholesalers and a product manager from a payments company, it had reached about ₹740 crore of annualised gross merchandise value by mid-2026, with 1.6 crore app installs and about 19 lakh buyers a year.

Its competitive position was awkward and profitable. Meesho and Flipkart were vastly larger and cheaper; Myntra and Ajio owned the branded end; Nykaa Fashion owned aspiration. Jhalak had found a seam between them — unbranded but curated, mid-priced at ₹1,200 to ₹4,500, and sold with the conviction of a human being on camera. Payments ran over UPI through a Razorpay integration, with cash on delivery offered in about 19,000 pincodes. A small wholesale arm shipped bulk consignments to diaspora retailers in the Gulf, the United States and Singapore.

The team was spread across six time zones. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune; Lena Brandt, the design lead, worked from Berlin; Priyanka Sundaram, the only full-time data scientist, had joined from Toronto in January and worked mornings that were Mumbai's evenings; Ivan Chua ran partnerships and customer success from Singapore; and Jaideep Bhalla sold the wholesale line out of New Jersey. Jhalak's largest single wholesale account was Deeba Trading, a Dubai group with eleven stores in Deira and Karama, whose owner Nusrat Qureshi placed consignment orders worth about ₹6 crore a year.

3. The situation

Two things had changed in April, within a fortnight of each other, and neither had been designed as an experiment.

On 8 April the mobile team in Pune shipped a rewritten live-video player, built to cut streaming cost by moving to adaptive bitrate. On 21 April, operations in Surat withdrew cash on delivery from about 11,000 of the 19,000 eligible pincodes — essentially everything outside the top eight cities and their satellite towns. The reason was sound: return-to-origin on cash-on-delivery orders had reached 18 per cent of shipments, and the reverse-logistics and re-packing cost was running at about ₹2.4 crore a month. After the withdrawal, return-to-origin fell to 11 per cent, saving roughly ₹14 crore on an annualised basis.

By June the repeat number was visibly down and the explanations had hardened into camps. Rakesh Iyer in Bengaluru believed the video player was at fault: buffering complaints in the Play Store had risen, and a stream that stutters is a shop where the shopkeeper keeps disappearing. Nikhil Warrier, who ran growth from Mumbai, believed nothing was wrong with the product at all — Jhalak had doubled the share of new buyers coming from coupon and cashback affiliates because they were cheap, and coupon buyers had never repeated well. Farida Contractor, who ran operations from Surat, believed both of them were looking for reasons to reverse her decision.

Priyanka Sundaram, working from Toronto, had spent three weeks building the only thing that could adjudicate: the same repeat-rate metric computed separately for each way of cutting the buyer base, with the size of every group reported beside its rate.

4. The people

Sneha Vaidya, Head of Product, Mumbai. Three years at Jhalak, previously at a fashion marketplace. She owns the festive plan and will present whatever she decides to the founders on 10 August. What she wants is to stop the repeat-rate decline without spending the festive engineering budget on the wrong thing.

Rakesh Iyer, Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. His team owns the player. He has asked for two sprints — six engineers for four weeks, about ₹38 lakh of loaded cost and the whole of the pre-festive engineering window — to rebuild the low-end playback path. He also, privately, does not want the player rewrite to be recorded as the cause of a ₹95 crore miss.

Nikhil Warrier, Head of Growth, Mumbai. Coupon and affiliate traffic has taken his blended cost of acquiring a buyer from ₹610 to ₹430, which is the number his bonus is measured against. He argues the repeat decline is arithmetic, not damage, and that cutting the channel before Diwali would leave the top of the funnel empty in the only season that matters.

Farida Contractor, Head of Operations, Surat. Twenty-two years in textile logistics. She withdrew cash on delivery and can show ₹14 crore of annualised savings for it. She points out that reinstating it before Diwali, when volumes triple, would put the reverse-logistics operation under strain it has never survived well.

5. Exhibits

Priyanka's first exhibit cut new buyers by how they were acquired. The rates are thirty-day repeat purchase among first-time buyers; the shares are of first-time buyers in each period.

Exhibit 1. Thirty-day repeat purchase by acquisition channel. Source: Jhalak event stream joined to attribution table; channel assigned at install and never revised. Periods: Dec 2025–Mar 2026 and Apr–Jul 2026.

The share-weighted rates reproduce the published aggregate in both periods, which told Priyanka the cut was clean. Nikhil was partly right: the coupon channel had gone from 12 to 26 per cent of intake, and it repeats at half the rate of creator-led buyers. But holding the old rates fixed and moving only the shares gives 28.4 per cent — a mix effect of 2.7 points. The remaining 3.9 points is a real fall inside the segments, and it is present in every channel.

To find the behavioural part, Priyanka held the channel constant and cut performance-marketing buyers — the largest stable segment — two further ways. Exhibit 3 cuts by device, which is the test of Rakesh's theory. Exhibit 4 cuts by whether the buyer's pincode kept cash on delivery, which is the test of Farida's.

Exhibit 3 does not support Rakesh. If the player rewrite were doing the damage, the loss would concentrate on low-memory Android devices; instead it is almost flat across device classes, with only a point of difference between the best and worst. Exhibit 4 is a different picture entirely. In pincodes that kept cash on delivery the repeat rate barely moved. In the pincodes where it was withdrawn, it fell by seven points — and those pincodes hold more than half of Jhalak's performance-marketing buyers.

6. The options

Option A: cut the coupon channel. Move the coupon and affiliate budget — about ₹4.2 crore a quarter — back into creator-led shows. Upside: it raises the reported repeat rate mechanically and buys better customers. Cost: creator-led acquisition costs about ₹780 per buyer against ₹310 for coupon traffic, so the same budget buys roughly 40 per cent fewer new buyers going into the largest season of the year, and it addresses only the 2.7 points that were never a defect.

Option B: rebuild the player. Give Rakesh his two sprints. Upside: playback quality on low-end devices is worth having regardless, and it protects against a risk the data may simply be too coarse to see. Cost: ₹38 lakh and the entire pre-festive engineering window, spent against a hypothesis that Exhibit 3 does not support.

Option C: restore a paid-on-delivery path in the withdrawn pincodes. Reinstate cash on delivery selectively, or replace it with a partial-prepayment option — a ₹99 token paid over UPI at checkout with the balance in cash — in the 11,000 pincodes, before the festive season. Upside: it acts directly on the segment where the loss is. Cost: reverse-logistics exposure returns, Farida's ₹14 crore saving is partly given back, and the operations team must absorb it at triple volume.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Why can no comparison of Jhalak's aggregate repeat rate before and after April distinguish between the three explanations, however carefully it is computed?

2. Nikhil's channel-mix argument is arithmetically correct. Why is it nonetheless an incomplete answer to Sneha's question, and what would make it a complete one?

3. Exhibit 3 shows the loss spread almost evenly across device classes. What would Exhibit 3 have to look like for Rakesh's theory to be supported, and what else should Sneha check before dismissing it?

4. What should Sneha take into Friday's plan lock, and what would she need to see by October to know she was wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is segmentation: the practice of refusing to reason about a metric until it has been computed separately for groups of users defined by an attribute, with the size of each group reported next to its rate. Jhalak's aggregate fell 6.6 points, and the aggregate alone is consistent with all three stories, because an aggregate is a share-weighted average and can move either because groups behaved differently or because the groups changed size.

A well-reasoned answer does three things in order. It decomposes the fall into a mix component and a within-segment component, which Exhibit 1 permits: 2.7 points came from coupon buyers rising from 12 to 26 per cent of intake, and 3.9 points is a genuine change in behaviour. It then holds the channel constant and cuts the within-segment loss by the attributes that correspond to the two candidate causes. And it checks that the parts reconcile to the whole — Exhibit 4's weighted rates reproduce Exhibit 1's performance-marketing row, which is what licenses the conclusion.

On those tests, one defensible path is Option C, scoped narrowly, with a piece of Option A attached. The evidence locates almost all of the behavioural loss in pincodes where cash on delivery was withdrawn: seven points lost there against 0.8 points where it was retained. Restoring a payment path in those pincodes — ideally the partial-prepayment variant, which keeps most of the return-to-origin saving because a buyer who has paid ₹99 rarely refuses the parcel — acts on the place the loss actually is. Sneha should pilot it in three states through September rather than reinstate everywhere, so that Farida's operation is not tested at festive peak on an untested policy.

Option A is not wrong, but it is a pricing decision rather than a repair. Coupon buyers repeat at 13 per cent, so they are worth roughly a third of a creator-led buyer over a year; the correct response is to bid for them accordingly, not to declare them a defect. Option B should not consume the festive window on this evidence, though Rakesh's instinct deserves one cheap test: Exhibit 3 uses a memory proxy, and a cut by network type and stream-abandonment rate would be a fairer trial of his theory before it is set aside.

The general lesson is the one Sneha put to the founders on 10 August: a segment tells you where a change happened, which is almost always enough to choose an action, and almost never enough to explain one. The seven-point fall in the withdrawn pincodes is a location, not yet a mechanism — and the team that confuses the two will fix the wrong thing with great confidence.

Jharokha Systems: the number on slide four

Bengaluru, Sunday 13 September 2026. Eight points have come off the company's headline engagement metric. Nobody in the building can say whether the product is failing, the customers are failing, or the measurement is.

1. Sunday night

Nandita Rao had the board deck open on one screen and, on the other, four queries that disagreed with it. It was a quarter past eleven on Sunday 13 September 2026. The board of Jharokha Systems met at half past nine the next morning in the company's office off 12th Main in Indiranagar, and slide four carried a single line that Nandita had written and could no longer defend: Weekly active outlets: 78.5% (Aug), from 86.5% (Mar).

Below it, in smaller type, sat the number the board would actually ask about. Net revenue retention had fallen from 114 per cent a year ago to 103 per cent in the six months to August. Vikram Sahni, the chief executive, had spent August in conversations about a Series D at a valuation near ₹2,600 crore, and the lead investor's indicative terms had a retention covenant in them. Nandita did not know the exact number in the covenant. She knew that Vikram had asked her, twice in ten days, whether the engagement fall was "real or a measurement thing", and that both times she had answered honestly — that she could not yet tell — and both times he had taken it as a yes to the second.

What she had in front of her instead was six exhibits, produced by five different systems, of which at least two could not both be true.

2. How Jharokha got here

Jharokha Systems was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Vikram Sahni and two engineers who had built billing software for a hotel group. The product was a restaurant operating system: a point-of-sale running on Android tablets on the counter, inventory and recipe costing, GST-compliant invoicing, a white-label ordering app for the outlet's own customers, loyalty, and connectors that pulled Swiggy and Zomato orders into the same ticket queue so that a kitchen in Kothrud or Kukatpally worked one screen instead of four.

By September 2026 it billed 9,200 outlets and ₹212 crore of annual recurring revenue. It employed 640 people: engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, design led from Berlin by a contractor the founders had met at a conference, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore for the international book, and a four-person sales beachhead in New Jersey pursuing Indian-origin restaurant groups in the United States.

One decision from November 2023 shaped everything that followed. To win Mandira Foodworks — a multi-brand chain then at 1,180 outlets, now at 1,460, and Jharokha's largest logo — the company agreed to a bespoke "enterprise edition". Mandira's security review would not permit the standard client-side analytics SDK, and its integration team insisted on the event schema as it stood in 2023, contractually frozen for the term. Jharokha said yes; the contract was worth ₹21 crore a year and it made the Series C. Three more enterprise accounts were subsequently signed on the same terms because the sales team had a template that worked.

The consequence, four years later, is that roughly 1,200 outlets — thirteen per cent of the base, forty-four per cent of the revenue — emit a different, older, thinner stream of events than everyone else, and several of the fields the product team now relies on do not exist in it at all. A migration to a unified taxonomy was funded in January 2025, re-scoped in August 2025 and again in April 2026, and is, by Arjun Bhatt's own most recent estimate, "about sixty per cent through the SMB tier and not started on enterprise".

3. The industry around it

The Indian restaurant-technology market in 2026 was crowded and margin-thin. Petpooja and Posist held enormous installed bases in the mid-market; UrbanPiper had made itself the default aggregator-integration layer; Dotpe, Pine Labs and Razorpay pressed in from payments; and Swiggy and Zomato each offered their own merchant tooling to the outlets they already served. Price pressure was constant: a single-outlet café in Nashik could be taken away for ₹400 a month.

Three forces were live. The Open Network for Digital Commerce had gone from curiosity to material volume for food delivery in 2025 and 2026, and outlets were discovering that an ONDC order carried a commission a third of what an aggregator charged. Every restaurant-tech vendor had rushed a network participant integration out; Jharokha's shipped in February 2026. Second, GST e-invoicing thresholds had come down again, pulling smaller outlets into compliance and making a compliant POS less optional. Third, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had finally bitten: diner-level data — phone numbers, order histories, loyalty identities — now sat under consent obligations that Jharokha's legal counsel in Mumbai read strictly, which meant that the company's richest potential segmentation axis, the diner rather than the outlet, was largely closed to it.

Internationally, Jharokha had 340 outlets outside India, of which 210 belonged to Nawras Hospitality, a Dubai group running food courts and casual-dining brands across the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Nawras was worth ₹9.4 crore a year, renewed on 31 March 2027, and had been asking since February for in-region data residency and proper Arabic right-to-left support in the counter application.

4. The situation, in sequence

The timeline matters because what was believed at each point has since changed.

February 2026. Jharokha shipped its ONDC integration. Adoption was slow and nobody watched it closely.

14 April 2026. Engineering released version 3 of the aggregator connector. It moved order ingestion from a synchronous webhook to a nightly reconciliation batch for outlets on the new connector — better for kitchen-display latency, cheaper to run, and, as nobody wrote down at the time, a change in where those orders appeared in Jharokha's own data. Orders reconciled in the batch land in the billing ledger but not in the product event stream. About 38 per cent of outlets were on v3 by August.

May 2026. Weekly active outlets, defined since 2022 as outlets processing at least twenty orders in a calendar week, began to slide. Nobody was alarmed; May is a slow month for dine-in.

June 2026. Meghna Pillai's team closed a strong quarter, largely on multi-outlet master agreements. Because such agreements bill from signature with a ninety-day ramp, roughly 600 outlets entered the billed denominator without a counter tablet in them.

July 2026. The blended weekly-active-outlet figure crossed below 80 per cent. Nandita asked Tanvi Kulkarni in Toronto to investigate. Tanvi's first finding was not about the product: the twenty-orders-a-week threshold had been chosen in 2022 when Jharokha's base was overwhelmingly dine-in, and it systematically classified small cloud kitchens — a fast-growing part of the self-serve tier — as inactive even when they were trading normally at twelve to fifteen orders a week.

19 August 2026. Faraz Siddiqui, chief technology officer at Nawras, wrote to Hui Ling Koh in Singapore saying that unless data residency and Arabic support had a committed date, Nawras would begin a vendor evaluation in October. Hui Ling logged it as a risk. The account's health score in the customer-success system remained green.

2 September 2026. Harish Menon's finance team closed August. Gross churn in the self-serve tier was 19 per cent annualised. The number had been 12 per cent a year earlier.

5. The people

Nandita Rao, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Position: the metric is unreliable and should not drive a decision this quarter. Incentive: she sponsored the taxonomy migration in 2025 and has defended its slipping dates three times. Not saying: she has known since June that the blended weekly-active-outlet number splices two incompatible definitions, and has continued to publish it because unsplicing it in a board deck would require explaining why it was ever spliced.

Vikram Sahni, co-founder and Chief Executive, Bengaluru. Position: the company needs one clear narrative for the raise and cannot afford a quarter of introspection. Incentive: the Series D. Not saying: the indicative term sheet is conditioned on net revenue retention, and he has not shown the condition to Nandita.

Harish Menon, Chief Financial Officer, Bengaluru. Position: billed outlets and recognised revenue are the only auditable facts; product analytics is "a telemetry hobby". Incentive: clean diligence. Not saying: his outlet count includes the roughly 600 ramp-clause outlets and about 190 outlets billed under minimum commitments at chains that have quietly shut them.

Meghna Pillai, Vice-President Sales, Mumbai. Position: this is competitive pressure; Petpooja and UrbanPiper are discounting and Jharokha should meet them with a retention programme. Incentive: her quota is bookings, not activation. Not saying: the ramp-clause structure that inflates the denominator was her idea, and she knows roughly how many of June's outlets are dark.

Arjun Bhatt, Head of Engineering, Pune. Position: nothing new gets instrumented until the migration is finished; any analysis built on today's schema will have to be rebuilt anyway. Incentive: protecting a team that has been asked to do two quarters of platform work while shipping ONDC. Not saying: the enterprise portion of the migration has no plan at all, because the Mandira contract's schema freeze may make it impossible without reopening a commercial negotiation.

Dr Tanvi Kulkarni, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: every current cut of the data is invalid; the segment definitions, the activity threshold and the denominator all need rebuilding before any conclusion is drawn. Incentive: she is on a two-year contract that ends in March 2027 and would like it converted. Not saying: she believes the correct unit of analysis is not the outlet at all but the order, by channel — and that saying so would obsolete a dashboard the whole company reads.

Hui Ling Koh, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Position: the health-score data shows enterprise stable and the risk concentrated in SMB; the product team is chasing a phantom. Incentive: her team's renewal targets and the quarterly business reviews they run. Not saying: health scores are entered by hand by customer-success managers, usually in the week before a review, and 41 per cent of them have not changed in two quarters.

Sandeep Gill, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Position: the India engagement debate is a distraction; the US pilot needs feature parity and three engineers. Incentive: a pipeline he has been building for a year. Not saying: he has been quoting Jharokha's India engagement numbers to American prospects, and a restatement would make his last four proposals inaccurate.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Outlet counts, August 2026, by source. Finance figures from the billing ledger as at 31 August; product figures from the analytics warehouse, counting outlets that emitted at least one order event in August on the current taxonomy. Nandita had drafted a sentence to that effect at eight o'clock and deleted it at half past ten.

7. Voices

"I don't need a philosophical position on measurement. I need to know whether outlets are using us less. If the answer is that we can't tell, then the answer we give the board is that we can't tell, and I'd rather not give that answer twice."

Vikram Sahni, leadership sync, Thursday 10 September

"Every one of these exhibits is computed over a different population. Exhibit 1 counts outlets we invoice. Exhibit 2 counts outlets that cross a threshold we picked for a business we no longer have. Exhibit 3 counts orders we can see, which since April is not the same as orders that happened. Exhibit 6 counts rupees, and excludes the one account that matters. We are not looking at a company. We are looking at four companies that share a logo."

Tanvi Kulkarni, memo to Nandita Rao, 8 September, 02:14 IST

"With respect, my CSMs are in those restaurants. Green means the operator picks up the phone and renews. I have thirty-four enterprise accounts and I can tell you the state of each one without a dashboard."

Hui Ling Koh, Singapore, on the weekly call

"Backfilling v3 into the warehouse is four weeks of two engineers, and those are the same two engineers who are the only ones who understand the SMB migration. You can have the backfill or you can have the migration finish this year. I have said this in three planning meetings."

Arjun Bhatt, Pune, chat thread #platform-planning

"We are losing single-outlet cafés to Petpooja at ₹400 a month. That is not an instrumentation problem, that is a price problem, and while we are counting things they are signing them."

Meghna Pillai, Mumbai, email to Vikram Sahni copied to Nandita Rao

"We have been patient. In Dubai the counter staff are Filipino, Egyptian and Indian, and the menu screens are in Arabic. Right-to-left is not a feature request; it is the language of the country. We will begin looking at alternatives in October unless there is a date."

Faraz Siddiqui, Nawras Hospitality, Dubai, 19 August

"Whatever you restate, please tell me before you restate it. I have four proposals in the market that quote eighty-seven per cent."

Sandeep Gill, New Jersey, direct message, 11 September

8. The options, as Nandita currently sees them

She had written three onto a card, in the order she thought of them, which was not necessarily the order of their merit.

Option A — declare the measurement broken. Withdraw weekly active outlets from board reporting, complete the taxonomy migration including the enterprise tier, backfill the v3 connector data, and rebuild the activity threshold on a defensible basis. Estimated ₹11 crore and two quarters of the platform team, and it requires reopening the Mandira schema clause. It buys a number nobody can argue with, in April, for a board meeting in September.

Option B — treat the fall as real and fight it. Accept the eight points as churn and competitive loss, and fund the retention programme Meghna wants: a self-serve price tier at ₹499, an onboarding concierge for new single outlets, and a win-back campaign. Roughly ₹9 crore. It is the only option that produces visible motion before Diwali, and it commits the company to a diagnosis that Exhibit 3 gives real reason to doubt.

Option C — re-segment with what exists. Do not wait for clean data. Publish the number three ways — by outlet, by order and by rupee — with stated definitions and honest ranges, and pick the tier with the clearest signal to act on first. Cheap in money, expensive in credibility, and it puts a range on slide four of a fundraising board deck.

What the card did not say, and what Tanvi's memo had said twice, was that all three options accept the outlet as the unit of analysis. Jharokha's customers were accounts, its revenue was rupees, its product was used by managers and its value was delivered in orders. The weekly active outlet was a measure invented in 2022 by three people in a room, for a base of dine-in restaurants that no longer resembled the company's base, and it had been on slide four ever since because it had always been on slide four. Nor did the card mention ONDC, whose orders had quadrupled while aggregator passthrough fell — two lines in Exhibit 3 that might be one story rather than two, and which, if they were one story, would mean that the outlets were not less active at all but that their business was moving into a channel Jharokha had itself built.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board met at 9.30 on Monday 14 September. Nandita had until then.

Money: ₹18 crore of discretionary engineering and go-to-market budget remained for the second half of the financial year, and the three options consumed ₹11 crore, ₹9 crore and almost nothing respectively. Headcount was frozen until the Series D closed. Tanvi's contract ran to March 2027 and she had told Nandita, without elaborating, that she had been approached.

Contracts: the Mandira schema freeze ran to March 2028 and reopening it meant reopening price. Nawras renewed on 31 March 2027 and wanted a data-residency commitment that required infrastructure in the UAE, which nobody had costed. Sandeep's American pipeline assumed feature parity that did not exist.

Regulation: the DPDP Act closed the diner-level segmentation that would have made the channel question easy to answer, and counsel had advised that consent collected by the outlet did not transfer to Jharokha for analytics purposes. GST e-invoicing changes due in January 2027 would consume some part of the same engineering capacity regardless of what was decided.

And the raise: whatever Nandita put on slide four would be read by an investor's diligence team in October, alongside every number the company had published for two years.

10. Questions for discussion

1. List the populations over which each of the six exhibits is computed. Which pairs of exhibits are being compared in the board deck as though they were computed over the same population, and what would it take to make any two of them comparable?

2. Exhibit 2 shows that the mix of tiers accounts for none of the eight-point fall. What would you need to know before accepting that conclusion, and which of the footnotes elsewhere in the exhibits bear on it?

3. Exhibits 2, 5 and 6 all suggest the enterprise tier is the healthiest part of the business. Construct the strongest case that it is the most endangered, using only evidence present in the case.

4. Tanvi argues that the outlet is the wrong unit of analysis. What would change in Jharokha's diagnosis if the unit were the order and the channel instead — and what would the company lose by abandoning a metric its whole organisation reads?

5. Each of the eight stakeholders has something they are not saying. Choose three, and trace what a decision taken in ignorance of each would cost the company over the following four quarters.

6. It is Monday morning. What does Nandita do first, what goes on slide four, and what does she say when a director asks whether the eight points are real?

At a quarter to one, Nandita closed the laptop and then opened it again. The cursor sat at the end of the line on slide four. She had three versions of the sentence saved in the speaker notes: one that reported the number, one that withdrew it, and one that reported it with a footnote she had rewritten four times and still did not believe. Outside, the last of the Ganesh visarjan traffic was moving down 100 Feet Road, and in Toronto it was still afternoon; Tanvi was online, and had been for some hours, and had not written anything further.

Segmenting Users in Analytics

A near-expert treatment: the arithmetic of decomposition, the schools that disagree about what a segment is for, the places where cutting a metric stops being informative and starts being actively misleading, and what separates a practitioner who slices well from one who merely slices.

1. Two decisions, both hanging on a cut

On 14 September 2026, Sharmila Iyengar, VP of product analytics at Manjistha Money, a personal-lending app operating under a non-banking finance licence, had four working days to answer a question her CEO, Vikram Nanda, had phrased in a way she disliked: "has our funnel got worse, or have our customers?" The metric in dispute was first-disbursal conversion — the share of applicants who complete KYC and receive money in their account within seventy-two hours. In April it had been 29.75% across 80,000 applicants. In August it was 26.53% across 120,000. Three points and a bit. Nanda's board believed it measured underwriting friction. Manjistha's risk committee believed it measured applicant quality. The lending business had grown 50% in volume over the same window, almost all of it through embedded placements inside partner apps and lead aggregators, and the two beliefs implied opposite actions: rebuild the KYC flow, or throttle the channels.

Eight hundred kilometres away and twelve days earlier, Anirudh Bhatt, VP of product at Indraneel Systems, faced a structurally identical problem wearing entirely different clothes. Indraneel sold an AI support agent to six enterprise accounts; its headline metric was autonomous resolution rate, the share of customer conversations closed without a human. In July, across two million conversations, that rate was 61.6%. Indraneel's pricing, its renewal conversations and one clause in its largest contract all referenced it. But Meera Sundaram, who ran customer success, kept reporting a different number in her own reviews: 68.0%. Neither was wrong. Bhatt's was the conversation-weighted mean; Sundaram's was the mean across accounts. The gap between them was not a data-quality defect. It was a choice about what the unit of analysis is, and it determined whether Indraneel's product looked like it was working for its customers or working for its biggest customer.

Both decisions turn on the same operation, and neither is resolved by it. Segmentation will tell Iyengar and Bhatt where their numbers moved. It will not tell either why — and, the part most practitioners under-appreciate, a careless cut can make both of them confidently wrong in a direction that looks rigorous.

2. The idea, and the four camps that will not agree about it

A segment is a partition of a population by an attribute, within which the same metric is recomputed on the same definition. It is worth being pedantic about each clause. Partition: the groups must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, so that the segmented results reconstruct the aggregate exactly. Attribute: a property of the user, account, session or event, as distinct from a cohort, which partitions by time of entry. Same metric, same definition: numerator, denominator and window held fixed, because a segmented number that redefines the denominator is not a decomposition, it is a different metric in a decomposition's clothing.

The lineage runs through marketing rather than statistics. Wendell Smith's 1956 distinction between market segmentation and product differentiation established the strategic claim: a market is several demand curves, not one. Yoram Wind's 1978 review added the criteria still used to referee a proposed segmentation — substantial, identifiable, reachable, stable and, above all, actionable, meaning that knowing a user belongs to it changes what you would do. Digital analytics inherited the vocabulary but changed its economics: where classical segmentation was expensive to measure and therefore reasoned about in advance, event-stream tooling made any slice nearly free, and the binding constraint shifted from data collection to inferential discipline. Statistics had meanwhile produced its own version of the same worry — Simpson's 1951 note on the reversal of associations under aggregation, and the shift-share decomposition literature in labour economics — both describing the mechanism that makes segmentation necessary: an aggregate rate is a weighted mean, and weighted means move for two reasons.

Four camps now argue about what follows, and a manager refereeing them should know exactly what each will and will not sign.

The decomposition school, strongest in operating and finance-adjacent analytics, will sign: no aggregate metric should be acted upon before it has been split into parts that reconcile arithmetically to it. It will not sign that the resulting parts identify causes. Its virtue is that bookkeeping is checkable.

The causal-inference school will sign: an observational segment difference is a hypothesis, and nothing more, because segment membership is itself chosen by behaviour and correlated with everything. It will not sign that a segment found in a dashboard justifies a product decision without a randomised or quasi-experimental test. Its adherents are the ones who point out that "power users retain better" is very close to a tautology.

The model-based school, ascendant in personalisation and uplift modelling, will sign: the discrete segment is a lossy compression of a continuous individual-level response surface, retained because humans cannot read a response surface. It will not sign that there is a correct number of segments, or that any boundary corresponds to something real. Ask it for "the three personas" and it answers that there are as many personas as users.

The strategic school, descended directly from Smith and Wind, will sign: a slice you cannot address with a different action is not a segment, it is a filter. It will not sign that statistical distinguishability confers status. It is the camp that kills the elegant four-way cut by asking what anyone would do differently on Monday.

The disagreement is not semantic. Iyengar's channel cut is a decomposition claim; her risk committee's reading of it is a causal claim; and Nanda's eventual question — "which of these can we act on?" — is the strategic one.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic of a moving weighted mean

An aggregate rate p is Σ wi pi, where wi is segment i's share of the denominator and pi its own rate. Between two periods, the change decomposes exactly into three terms:

Δp = Σ wi0Δpi (the rate, or within, effect) + Σ pi0Δwi (the mix, or between, effect) + Σ ΔpiΔwi (the interaction).

Most practitioners know the first two terms and quietly discard the third, or use a two-term variant assigning the interaction to one side by convention. That is defensible when shares move a point or two; it is not when a channel doubles, which is precisely the situation in which anyone bothers to decompose.

The within term is 0.500(−0.5) + 0.375(−1.0) + 0.125(−2.0) = −0.875 points. The mix term is 34.0(−0.150) + 28.0(+0.025) + 18.0(+0.125) = −2.15 points. The interaction is (−0.5)(−0.150) + (−1.0)(0.025) + (−2.0)(0.125) = −0.20 points. The three sum to −3.225, exactly the observed change. Two-thirds of Manjistha's decline is mix: the company did not get much worse at converting any particular kind of applicant, it bought many more of the kind it converts badly. The interaction term, small in size, carries the most managerial content — it says the aggregator channel degraded and grew at once, the signature of a channel scaled past the depth of its quality inventory.

Three steps are usually left implicit, and each is where competent work separates from careless. The first is fixing the assignment rule before the cut: when is a user's channel decided — first touch, last touch, at application, or re-derived at query time? Manjistha's warehouse re-derived it on last touch at query time, so a user who arrived through an aggregator and later opened the app organically silently migrated segments between two pulls of the same historical month. The second is auditing residuals: Manjistha's "unattributed" bucket was 4% of April applicants and 9% of August, and had been excluded from the dashboard's chart; nine per cent of the denominator at an unknown rate can carry much of a three-point move. The third is deciding the unit of analysis explicitly, which is Bhatt's entire problem.

4. When the decomposition earns its keep, and when it misleads

The conditions can be stated as testable claims, each of which can be checked against both companies before any conclusion is drawn.

Claim one: segment shares moved materially. If every wi is stable to within a point, the mix term is negligible and decomposition is ceremony. At Manjistha, aggregator share doubled from 12.5% to 25.0%; the claim holds emphatically. At Indraneel, the account mix was stable in July, but Kumkum Beauty's share of conversations had risen from 41% to 52% over two quarters as it migrated more queues onto the platform — so the claim holds there too, on a longer horizon than Bhatt was looking at.

Claim two: segments differ in level by more than they differ in noise. A cut whose segments sit within sampling error of each other explains nothing, however satisfying it looks. Manjistha's channels differ by up to 17 points on tens of thousands of applicants; Indraneel's accounts by 20 points on hundreds of thousands of conversations each — though, as the nuances below argue, its effective sample is closer to the number of accounts than of conversations.

Claim three: the segment is actionable — some lever moves differently across it. Manjistha can throttle a channel, reprice it, or route its applicants to a different underwriting path. This is exactly where the platform cut in most consumer companies fails: knowing Android converts worse than iOS is true and unactionable unless it decomposes further into something a team controls.

Claim four: segment membership is not caused by the outcome. This is where segmentation turns actively misleading. If a segment is defined on behaviour downstream of the metric — "users who completed onboarding", "accounts with an active integration", "conversations that reached the second turn" — the comparison conditions on a collider and manufactures differences out of selection. A team reporting that "integrated accounts churn at a third the rate" has usually discovered that accounts which intended to stay took the trouble to integrate.

The sharpest misleading case is aggregation reversal. Inside Manjistha's aggregator channel, Iyengar cut by employment type and found something that stopped the argument in the room.

Iyengar's conclusion was that both readings in Nanda's office were artefacts of stopping the cut one level too early. The channel was not degrading; its supply had shifted toward self-employed applicants, whose documentation burden under the lender's own KYC rules was genuinely heavier, and for whom conversion was structurally lower and slightly improving.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Indraneel's case is the AI-native edge case in its purest form, and it begins with the unit of analysis. The metric is defined over conversations; the customer relationship, the contract and the churn risk are defined over accounts; the human experience is defined over end users Indraneel never sees, because they belong to its customers.

Table 3 — Indraneel Systems, autonomous resolution by account, July 2026

Two-sided and multi-product situations generalise the defect. Haldiya Mandi, an agricultural trading marketplace, computes a match rate whose numerator is buyer-side and denominator seller-side; a cut on a buyer attribute silently redefines the denominator and the segments stop reconciling. The honest practice is to segment each side separately and treat the joint metric as a function of two segmented distributions. In a multi-product company the seam is subtler: a user of two products belongs to two schemes, so any company-wide "active user" cut must decide whether it partitions users or user-product pairs. Both are legitimate; mixing them in one table is not.

Regulated and hardware contexts add constraints that are not analytical at all. Manjistha cannot segment on certain protected or inferred attributes for underwriting-adjacent decisions; even where a cut is permitted for diagnosis, using it to drive differential treatment crosses a line compliance polices. Neelambari Grid Systems, whose smart meters run firmware on a two-to-four-year replacement cycle, has a problem with no software analogue: firmware version is confounded with hardware generation, install date, discom contract and geography at once, and none of it was independently assigned. Lakhaa Diagnostics, pairing an instrument with cloud software in clinical settings, faces both.

What mature companies say they do is maintain a governed segment taxonomy. What they actually do is govern the six or seven cuts that appear in board reporting and tolerate a long tail of team-local definitions elsewhere, on the reasonable ground that centralising everything would freeze exploration. The workable compromise, and the one Bhatt adopted, is a small registry of certified segments with owners, versions and change logs, plus a convention that any number leaving a team either uses them or says it does not.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Segment membership is a measurement, and measurements drift. The tell-tale sign is that a query over a fixed historical window returns different segment counts when re-run a month later. Last-touch attribution, retrained persona models and backfilled classifiers all rewrite the past. The obvious reading — that the data is "getting better" — is wrong in the way that matters: a comparison across two periods is only valid if membership was assigned by the same rule at the same point in each user's life, and re-derivation at query time quietly violates that.

The interaction term is where the story lives. The tell is a decomposition whose two components sum to exactly 100% of the change with no residual, which means someone has used a two-term form and assigned the cross-product by convention. The obvious reading is that the residual is a rounding artefact. It is not: a large negative interaction term is the specific signature of a segment simultaneously growing and degrading, which is what channel saturation, sales-motion overreach and capacity strain all look like in arithmetic.

The unit of analysis determines the answer more than the cut does. The tell is two teams reporting the same named metric several points apart, each able to reproduce theirs. Expert practice is to put the weighting in the metric's name — "conversation-weighted resolution", "account-mean resolution" — and pick the one matching the decision: churn wants account weighting, infrastructure cost wants volume weighting. The obvious reading, that one team's pipeline is broken, wastes a week.

Effective sample size is not row count. The tell is a confidence interval computed on two million conversations that come from six accounts. Observations clustered within accounts are correlated, so the effective n is closer to the number of clusters; Indraneel's per-account rates differ far more than binomial noise on hundreds of thousands of conversations could explain, which is itself the proof the clustering is real. Treating conversations as independent yields intervals an order of magnitude too narrow and makes every difference look significant.

Segments defined downstream of the outcome are not segments. The tell is a segment name containing a verb the product wanted performed: activated, integrated, invited a teammate. The obvious reading is that these are the behaviours to encourage; the problem is that membership is post-treatment, so the comparison estimates selection, not effect. The disciplined version defines membership from attributes fixed before the outcome window opens.

Power is consumed multiplicatively by each additional cut. The tell is a three- or four-way cross-tab presented to two decimal places. Splitting 120,000 applicants by channel (3), employment type (2), city tier (3) and device (2) yields thirty-six cells averaging 3,300, but the distribution is skewed and the smallest hold a few hundred. At n = 300 and p = 0.27 the standard error is about 2.6 points, so two cells can differ by seven points with no underlying difference at all.

Searching many cuts guarantees finding some. The tell is a finding introduced with "we sliced it every way and found that…". With sixty-four cells, roughly three will clear a 5% threshold under the null, and the expected largest |z| among sixty-four independent draws is around 2.7 — so a z of 2.3, which looks compelling in isolation, is less extreme than pure noise would typically produce. The remedy is not to stop exploring but to label exploratory findings as leads and confirm them in an independent period or a held-out split.

A segment's size changing discontinuously is a data event, not a business event. The tell is a step change in segment population on a single date that coincides with a deploy, a classifier retrain or a taxonomy migration. The obvious reading — that behaviour shifted — is almost never right. An expert checks whether the segment's denominator moved that day before interpreting its rate, because definitional change shows up in counts first.

The mean of segment rates is not the rate of the population. The tell is a "Total" row that is the arithmetic mean of the column above it. Indraneel's 68.0% is exactly this — a legitimate statistic about accounts, illegitimate as a claim about conversations. The error survives in senior reporting because the two numbers are usually close enough not to raise an eyebrow, until one segment gets large and the gap becomes a governance problem.

The cut a team reaches for usually mirrors the org chart, not the causal structure. The tell is that growth-owned metrics get cut by channel, platform-owned metrics by device, and nobody cuts by the thing that crosses both. Manjistha's true fault line — documentation burden for self-employed applicants — belonged to underwriting policy, which owned no dashboard. The obvious reading, that the available cuts are the relevant ones, is how organisations reliably fail to find causes that live between teams.

Observational heterogeneity does not transfer to experimental heterogeneity. The tell is "this feature helps power users more", supported by a comparison of users who were never randomised. Segment differences are estimable as effects only for subgroups defined before randomisation on pre-treatment attributes, and even then they are noisy: detecting an interaction typically needs roughly four times the sample of the main effect it modifies. The obvious reading treats a dashboard split as a subgroup analysis; it is not one.

7. How this differs across product types and stages

In consumer products with high volume, segmentation is cheap, granular and dangerous mostly through multiplicity. In B2B and enterprise it is expensive, coarse and dangerous mostly through clustering: with six or sixty accounts, the account is the observation, and a single large customer's behaviour is indistinguishable from a product trend. This is the one place where the difference between business models is genuinely qualitative rather than a matter of degree — everywhere else, the mechanics are identical and only the sample sizes change.

Platforms and marketplaces differ in one specific respect: their headline metrics are ratios across two populations, so a single-sided cut breaks reconciliation and the right object of segmentation is usually a local market — a city, a category, a route — rather than a user attribute. Hardware-plus-software companies differ because their most explanatory segment, device generation, is perfectly confounded with time; the practical response is to cohort on install date and treat generation as a fixed effect rather than a finding. AI products differ because their natural segment is the request — intent, language, difficulty — and because the model itself generates boundaries that move on every retrain, so definitions there need version pinning that a channel definition does not.

By stage, only which error dominates changes. An early company has cells too thin for inference and should triangulate with qualitative evidence rather than pretend a thirty-user cell is a finding. A scaled company has unlimited slicing capacity, several incompatible definitions of "enterprise" or "power user", and a reporting surface wide enough that somewhere on it, every week, a false positive reaches someone senior. The arithmetic does not change: the decomposition identity holds at any size, and reconciliation costs the same at either.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

The first is Manjistha's, already worked: a three-point aggregate fall that was two-thirds mix, with a within-channel reversal in which both employment sub-segments improved. The payoff was that the two competing explanations in Nanda's office were both refuted and a third, which nobody had proposed, was supported.

The second is Indraneel's. Bhatt did not choose between 61.6% and 68.0%. He decomposed Kumkum Beauty's 54.0% by intent and found order-tracking at 62.0% on 70% of volume, refunds and returns at 40.0% on 22%, and payment failures at 24.0% on 8% — which reconciles to 54.1%, the residual being rounding. The seventeen-point account gap was not a quality gap at all; it was a mix gap. Kumkum's queue composition was unusually heavy in refunds, the category where Indraneel's agent needed write access to a system it had not been granted. The renewal risk was real, the product defect was specific, and the fix was an integration scope change rather than a model improvement. Bhatt's reporting change was to publish both means side by side with a per-account intent-mix table beneath them.

The third failed. In June, Haldiya Mandi's growth team, investigating a flat quarter, cut seller conversion sixty-four ways across category, geography, tenure and listing type. One cell — traders in a single onion-producing belt, n = 180 — showed 19.4% against a 27.0% baseline. The standard error at that size is 3.3 points, giving z = 2.30 and a nominal p near 0.021, which the team read as decisive. Eleven engineering weeks went into a category-specific listing flow. It moved nothing. The post-mortem found two faults stacked. First, multiplicity: across sixty-four cells a z of 2.30 was not merely survivable under the null, it was close to what the null predicts as a maximum. Second, definitional drift: the trader-category field had been backfilled by a new classifier on 3 June, moving roughly 40% of that cell in or out, so part of the collapse was reclassification. Recovery had three parts — a pre-registered list of cuts agreed before each investigation, a rule that any exploratory cell must reproduce in a fresh period before entering a roadmap, and a registry recording when every definition changed. The registry caught two further phantom findings within a quarter, which is the honest measure of its value.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Chasing the loudest swing rather than the largest contribution. Early sign: percentage changes cited without denominators in a standup. Diagnostic question: how many points of the aggregate move does this segment actually explain? Cost of catching it late is an engineering quarter, as at Haldiya Mandi.

Treating a mix shift as a quality decline. Early sign: a remediation plan aimed at a segment whose own rate never fell. Diagnostic: run the three-term decomposition before proposing a fix. Caught late, the cost is a redesign that cannot work, plus the loss of the actual lever — acquisition policy — for another cycle.

Non-reconciling segments. Early sign: an "other" or "unattributed" bucket omitted from the chart. Diagnostic: do the weighted segment rates reproduce the headline to the decimal? Caught late, an entire analysis is retracted in front of a board, which costs credibility that takes quarters to rebuild.

Definition drift mistaken for behaviour change. Early sign: a segment's population steps on a deploy date. Diagnostic: plot segment size, not just segment rate, and overlay the pipeline change log. Late cost: decisions compounded on a phantom trend.

Circular segments. Early sign: a persona whose definition includes the outcome being explained. Diagnostic: could a user's membership have been determined before the measurement window opened? Late cost: a strategy built on a tautology, which is unusually hard to dislodge because every new analysis confirms it.

Unit-of-analysis collision. Early sign: two reproducible values for one metric name. Diagnostic: state the weighting in the name. Late cost: a contractual metric that means different things to the two parties who signed it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Pre-registered cuts versus automated discovery. The discipline camp argues that exploratory slicing has a false-discovery rate nobody controls and that the fix is a short list agreed in advance. The discovery camp argues, with evidence, that the most valuable segments in most companies were in nobody's hypothesis list — behavioural clusters and odd temporal patterns are routinely trawled and routinely real — and that correction procedures applied to correlated cells are so conservative they reject true findings wholesale. The discipline camp would be wrong if held-out replication showed a high share of trawled findings survive; the discovery camp would be wrong if audits showed most evaporate, which Haldiya Mandi's post-mortem suggests but one post-mortem cannot establish.

Centralised semantic layers versus local ownership. Centralisers point to the recurring failure in which "enterprise account" means three things in three dashboards and a board number cannot be reproduced. Localists answer that a certified definition is a snapshot of one team's question, that freezing definitions slows the discovery of better ones, and that the real cost of governance is the analyses nobody bothered to run. The position turns on how much of a firm's analytic value comes from reporting versus discovery, which genuinely differs.

Discrete segments versus individual-level models. The model camp holds that segments are a legacy of the era before individual prediction was cheap, and that uplift models estimating per-user treatment effects strictly dominate any partition. The segmentation camp responds that a per-user score is not a decision: organisations act through policies, policies are discrete, and a model whose logic cannot be stated in a sentence cannot be argued with in a room — and that individual effect estimates are extremely noisy, their apparent precision largely artefactual. The model camp would be wrong if uplift-derived policies failed to beat simple segment policies in holdout; the segment camp would be wrong if they consistently did.

Whether mix should be adjusted out of headline metrics. Reporting a mix-adjusted conversion rate — holding channel shares at a base period — makes product quality legible and is standard practice in retail's same-store-sales convention. The opposing view is blunt: the business really did convert 26.53%, the mix shift was a decision someone made, and adjusting it away lets acquisition strategy escape accountability by hiding inside a methodology. Both positions are held by serious people. The reconciling practice, which not everyone accepts, is to publish both and never the adjusted figure alone.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces the cut. Someone who has internalised it asks first what decision the answer will change, and often declines to cut at all because no available segment maps to a lever. They state the unit of analysis unprompted. They check the denominator's history before interpreting the rate's. They report the interaction term rather than distributing it. They can say which findings are confirmatory and which are leads, and they do not let the second kind into a roadmap without replication. They know the three or four cuts that have ever explained anything in their business and enter the rest of the search space deliberately and briefly. Most tellingly, they are comfortable saying a metric moved and the cut did not locate it — which means the explanatory attribute is not yet in the schema, and the next step is to construct it, not to keep slicing what is already there.

12. What each of them decided

Iyengar's recommendation to Nanda on 18 September was that Manjistha was not facing a funnel problem or a quality problem in the terms either side had argued. Conversion for salaried and self-employed aggregator applicants had both improved; the aggregate fell because self-employed applicants, for whom the company's own documentation requirements were heavier, had risen from 40% to 70% of that channel. The recommendation was therefore threefold: report conversion mix-adjusted and raw, side by side, permanently; commission a redesign of the self-employed documentation path, whose addressable population had tripled; and give the growth team a segment-level conversion floor rather than a blended one, so that scaling a channel past its quality depth would show up in the channel's own number rather than in the company's.

Bhatt stopped arguing about which mean was correct and changed what Indraneel measured. Resolution rate would be published account-weighted for renewal and health reviews and conversation-weighted for cost and capacity, each named accordingly, with an intent-mix table beneath. The contractual metric in the Kumkum Beauty agreement was renegotiated to be intent-normalised, since neither party wanted a number that moved when Kumkum migrated a new queue. The roadmap item that emerged was not a model improvement but a write-scope integration for refund workflows — a conclusion no aggregate, and no account cut alone, would have produced.

Discussion questions

1. Iyengar proposes publishing both mix-adjusted and raw conversion. What incentives does each number create for the growth team, and which of the two should appear in the board deck's headline?

2. Indraneel's largest account holds 52% of conversations. At what share does an account stop being a segment of the business and become the business — and what should Bhatt's reporting do differently at that point?

3. Haldiya Mandi's team followed a finding that was nominally significant. Given that pre-registration would also have prevented several genuine discoveries, what rule would you actually impose, and what would you accept losing?

13. Going deeper

Cohort analysis — the time-based sibling of segmentation; it isolates the one confound segmentation cannot, namely that different users entered at different moments under different conditions. It unlocks the ability to read whether a segment difference is a quality difference or a vintage effect.

Root cause analysis of a metric change — the disciplined continuation of everything above, once a segment is located; it turns "where" into "why" through funnel breakdowns and instrumentation forensics, and it is where the cut stops being sufficient.

Heterogeneous treatment effects — segmentation under randomisation, where the differences are estimable as effects rather than associations; it unlocks defensible personalisation and targeted rollout, and it is the formal answer to the tenth nuance above.

Constructing a funnel — supplies the intermediate denominators a segmented conversion metric decomposes into; without it, a segment difference has no mechanism attached.

Reading drop-off — teaches which step of a funnel a segment's deficit sits in, which is usually the difference between a policy fix and an interface fix.

Defining activation (the aha moment) — a segment boundary that is itself an outcome; studying it carefully is the best inoculation against the post-treatment segment error.

Retention curves and the PMF signal — the metric most often segmented, and the one where mix effects are most frequently mistaken for quality effects.

Stickiness and natural frequency — explains why two segments with genuinely different usage rhythms should not be judged on a shared window, a common source of false segment gaps.

Feature adoption analysis — the most common downstream application of a persona cut, and the place where circular segment definitions do the most damage.

Segmenting Users in Analytics

Where, exactly, did the change happen — on which platform, through which channel, to which kind of user, in which cohort? That question, asked before any question about why, is what segmentation exists to answer.

A number that will not sit still

On the morning of 9 March 2026, Ananya Kulkarni opened the retention dashboard at Trishul Mart, a ten-minute grocery delivery company operating across nine Indian cities, and found the seven-day repeat-order rate sitting at 37%. Three weeks earlier it had been 42%. Trishul Mart was seven weeks from closing a Series D, and the number due in the data room on 19 March was this one: the share of first-time customers who place a second order within a week of their first, the single metric the company's investors had told its CEO, Arjun Sabharwal, they cared about more than gross merchandise value. A five-point fall, unexplained, would read as a company losing product-market fit at the exact moment it was asking for more capital.

Ananya, Trishul Mart's head of product analytics, had one instinct and one constraint. The instinct was that a five-point drop in a blended, company-wide average almost never means the whole company got five points worse; usually some identifiable slice got much worse while the rest held steady, and the average hides that. The constraint was time: the board deck was due in ten days, and Sabharwal wanted a one-paragraph explanation, not a data-science seminar. What Ananya needed to do first was not run an experiment or interview customers. She needed to cut the number.

The idea

Segmentation, in analytics, is the practice of splitting an aggregate metric into the subgroups that make it up — by platform, by acquisition channel, by user persona, by signup cohort, or by any other attribute a user or event carries — and recomputing the same metric separately for each subgroup, so a single blended figure becomes a small map of where the underlying behaviour actually differs. It exists to solve a recurring failure: an average can move, or stay still, for reasons that have nothing to do with any individual group's behaviour changing, because averages blend groups of different sizes and different rates together. The practice descends from market segmentation, the idea that a market is not one customer but several distinct ones, which the marketing scholar Wendell Smith formalised in a 1956 paper distinguishing it from product differentiation. Digital product analytics adopted the same logic in the 2000s and 2010s, as web and mobile analytics tools made it cheap to slice an event stream by device, source and user property rather than report only a site-wide total, and it is now a default operation in every product analytics tool a Trishul Mart or its peers would use. The topic sits next to cohort analysis, and the two are easy to conflate: a cohort groups users by when something happened to them — the week they signed up — while a segment groups them by what they are — platform, channel, persona. In practice the two combine constantly, because a cohort is itself often one axis of a larger segmentation. The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "before we ask why the number moved, we ask where it moved — because until we know which platform, channel, persona or cohort actually changed, any explanation for why is a guess."

How it actually works

The mechanics are simple to state and easy to do badly. First, fix the metric's definition exactly — numerator, denominator, time window — and hold it fixed across every cut; Ananya's metric was repeat orders within seven days of a first order, divided by first-time customers in the cohort, measured only once the cohort had matured past day seven. Second, choose the dimensions to cut by: for Trishul Mart these were platform (iOS versus Android), channel (organic, performance marketing, referral), persona (a behavioural cluster distinguishing occasional top-up shoppers from weekly basket shoppers), and cohort (signup week). Third, for each dimension, split the population into mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive groups — every user in exactly one group, none left as "unknown" and silently dropped — and recompute the identical metric inside each. This is the step practitioners most often skip under time pressure, and the one that makes a segmentation trustworthy: if the segmented numbers do not sum back to the blended total, the cut is wrong, not the story.

The fourth step is one a newcomer rarely hears named: separating a rate effect from a mix effect. A blended average can fall because a segment's own rate fell, or because a low-rate segment simply became a larger share of the population, with no individual user behaving worse than before. Both look identical in the topline number; only a decomposition tells them apart, and the two call for different responses — one is a product problem inside a segment, the other a change in acquisition mix no product fix can touch. Fifth, before drawing conclusions: check segment size, not only rate. A dramatic swing from forty users is noise dressed as insight; a modest swing from twenty thousand may be the whole story.

A worked example, run twice

Start with the raw arithmetic. Trishul Mart's February cohort — customers who placed a first order in the first week of February — numbered 50,000, of whom 21,000 placed a second order within seven days: 21,000 / 50,000 = 42.0%. The March cohort numbered 60,000, of whom 22,200 repeated: 22,200 / 60,000 = 37.0%. Five points, exactly as the dashboard showed, and nothing in that pair of numbers says anything about cause.

Cut by platform. In February, iOS carried 20,000 of the 50,000 users; of those same 20,000 iOS users, 46.0% retained (9,200 repeat orders). Android carried the remaining 30,000 at 39.33% (11,800 repeat orders), and 9,200 + 11,800 = 21,000 reconciles exactly to the blended total. In March, iOS grew to 22,000 users holding at roughly 45.0% (9,900 repeat orders), essentially flat and within ordinary week-to-week noise. Android grew to 38,000 users, and by subtraction (22,200 total minus 9,900 from iOS) produced 12,300 repeat orders — a rate of 12,300 / 38,000 = 32.37%, a fall of nearly seven points from February's 39.33%, worse than the whole-company drop, because Android's larger and growing share of the cohort (60% of the total in February, 63.3% in March) let its own decline pull the blended number down further than the decline alone would suggest. Rate effect and mix effect were compounding: Android got worse, and Android also became a bigger share of the business, so the topline absorbed both hits at once.
